analysis.one_liner: Bans common credit card fees and interest charges, caps penalty rate hikes, and forces regulator audits of card issuers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor vote; it was introduced with no cosponsors and died in the House Financial Services Committee when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the rules for credit cards. Card companies could not charge interest on balances you pay on time, could not raise your interest rate on money you already borrowed, could raise a penalty rate only seven points above your current rate, and could not stack over-the-limit fees on top of fees they themselves added. Your payments would have to go first to the balance with the highest interest rate, federal regulators would audit card companies every year, and regulators would report to Congress on how much money card operations make off interest and fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card holders, especially people who carry balances, who would pay less in interest and fees and see fewer surprise rate hikes.

how_it_helps.text: Card companies could not charge interest on debt a customer paid on time or paid in full within the grace period, ending so-called double-cycle and residual-interest billing. [S3]

Interest rate increases on an open account would be barred unless the customer agreed in writing, the rate was a disclosed introductory or variable rate, or a penalty rate applied — and a penalty rate could not exceed seven percentage points above the prior rate. [S3]
Any rate increase would apply only to future borrowing, so card companies could not reprice balances customers had already rung up. [S3]

Card companies could not charge interest on fees, could not charge over-the-limit fees caused by their own late or over-limit fees, could charge an over-limit fee only once per billing cycle, and could not charge a fee just to pay a bill by mail, phone, or online. [S3]
Payments would have to be applied first to the highest-interest balance, minimizing finance charges instead of maximizing them. [S3]

Federal regulators would have to audit card issuers' operations annually, checking samples of billing statements and accounts to catch misapplied payments and fees, and require corrective action. [S3]

The Federal Reserve would have to report annually to Congress on the profitability of card operations, including how much income comes from interest above 25 percent and from fees on cardholders and merchants. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Card-issuing banks, which would lose revenue from penalty rates, retroactive rate hikes, interest on fees, and over-limit and payment fees, plus the cost of annual audits and new payment-handling procedures.

drawbacks.text: Capping penalty rates and barring retroactive rate increases means issuers bear more risk on customers who stop paying on time; issuers would likely respond by charging higher standard rates, tightening approval, or adding up-front charges, which shifts costs back toward all borrowers, including those who pay on time. [S3]

Requiring annual regulator audits of every card issuer's operations, with sample reviews of statements and accounts, adds compliance and oversight costs that issuers would pass on to customers through pricing. [S3]
The bill took an unusually long time to reach the floor even by the standards of the period, and more comprehensive credit card legislation was advancing separately in Congress at the same time. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real and later became law in similar form, so the core benefits are proven rather than theoretical. The costs are real but standard for any credit regulation: some of the lost fee and interest revenue would be recouped through higher standard rates or tighter lending, hitting riskier borrowers hardest. The bill's yearly regulator audits were heavier than what comparable proposals required and would have been a legitimate target for trimming. On balance the benefits to cardholders plausibly outweighed the costs, but the bill attracted no cosponsors and never got a serious hearing, so it was never tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the same day in February 2008, the committee never scheduled a vote on it, and the bill died there when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Lincoln Davis introduced the bill on February 7, 2008. [S5]
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services. [S5]
That referral was the bill's last action; the committee took it up for no markup and no vote, and no floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers kept collecting the interest charges, penalty-rate hikes, retroactive rate increases, and stacking fees the bill would have banned, with no committee vote or floor vote ever taking place.

for.name: Rep. Lincoln Davis
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on February 7, 2008 and never scheduled a markup or vote on it, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Card issuing banks and the credit card industry
against.role: Card issuers subject to the bill's fee, rate, and audit rules
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions of this kind during the late-2000s credit card fight through lobbying against fee and rate limits.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote to measure party support; the sole sponsor was a Democrat, no one else signed on, and the bill died in a committee controlled by the House Democratic majority.

industries.note: The bill targets issuers' most profitable practices: charging interest on balances already paid, raising rates retroactively, stacking over-limit fees, and charging fees to make payments. Issuers' gains on these items come directly out of cardholders' bills, so the industry's interest ran against the bill. [S3]
The bill would give primary federal regulators an annual audit duty over card operations and enforcement responsibility for unfair practices, expanding their workload and oversight role. [S3]
